extracted.intended_audience: University of Virginia community, current and aspiring student journalists, and general readers interested in campus journalism and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflective criteria for student journalists covering high-profile, sensitive campus allegations — focusing on verification, community responsibility, emotional labor, and legal/ethical considerations. Drawn from a retrospective on coverage of a retracted national article and its campus impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and corroborate all relevant parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should contact alleged attackers, friends quoted in an account, and multiple witnesses rather than relying on a single account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Washington Post and other reviewers critiqued Erdely for not contacting Jackie’s alleged attackers or the friends who allegedly met Jackie; student reporters noted Erdely never reached out to a friend who was quoted in the article. Failure to contact relevant parties contributed to inconsistencies and eventual retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on a single source
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not build a consequential narrative based primarily on one main source without independent verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone partially then fully retracted the piece citing a loss of faith in its main source. The article stresses that reliance on a single uncorroborated account can cause major journalistic failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify factual claims against institutional records
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-check claims with institutional facts such as event schedules, police reports, and organizational records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phi Kappa Psi's internal investigation found no events the night of the alleged assault and noted pledging activities do not occur in the fall; such checks undermined the original story's timeline and contributed to exposing reporting holes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism and letting authorial opinion leak into narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain factual distance; do not let narrative voice, stereotypes, or an author's apparent delight in portraying a place influence the reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cavalier Daily leaders reviewed how Erdely’s opinions leaked through narrative style, saying it 'created an inaccurate presentation of University culture' and that the author appeared to 'delight' in stereotyping U.Va.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate personal feelings from reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters embedded in the community must consciously step back and distinguish facts from their own emotional reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alumni said it was hard to 'take a step back and look at the facts versus your feelings' when friends or classmates were involved; the piece repeatedly emphasizes the emotional difficulty of reporting while part of the affected community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presuppose the story; let reporting determine the narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Start reporting without a preformed narrative; avoid 'already knowing the story you want to tell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted student editors warned that coming in with the story you want to tell is 'an irresponsible way of reporting' — reporters 'really have to do the reporting and figure out what the story is, not the other way around.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local/embedded perspective responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage the paper’s embedded lens to offer context the national press may miss, but retain scrutiny and verification responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staffers argued their embedded perspective allowed them to offer insights national reporters could not, but also acknowledged that being part of the community complicated impartial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document administrative responses, activism, and campus consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly cover institutional actions (investigations, suspensions, policy changes), protests, and community activism as part of reporting the full story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cavalier Daily focused on documenting university responses, press conferences, student activism, administration actions (e.g., fraternity suspensions, Title IX policy revisions), and legal suits arising from the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the impact of coverage on survivors and public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether reporting might discourage survivors from coming forward or harm public trust in advocacy efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the retraction, staff worried the backlash might 'discourage other survivors from sharing their stories'; reporters should weigh potential chilling effects when covering unverified allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent and correct the record when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge reporting failures, publish corrections or statements interrogating coverage decisions, and follow up on retractions and their implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the retraction, The Cavalier Daily's managing board published a statement critiquing coverage; the article notes the importance of interrogating how narrative and opinion affected reporting and acknowledging mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate logistics for sustained legal or high-profile coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize staff schedules and shifts to ensure consistent courtroom and trial coverage despite student reporters’ conflicting commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During Eramo’s trial, news editors coordinated shifts so at least one Cavalier Daily reporter could be in the courthouse whenever possible — an 'all-hands-on-deck' approach for major legal events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply knowledge of media law when covering defamation cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand First Amendment, libel, and defamation principles when reporting on or attending related trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One reporter said attending the trial while learning First Amendment law helped connect classroom defamation concepts to real-world coverage; reporters should be aware of legal standards affecting reporting and litigation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for and mitigate online scrutiny and harassment of journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate intense public attention and potential personal attacks when covering emotionally charged stories; provide support for staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff members faced intense scrutiny and personal attacks online due to controversial coverage; the piece highlights the emotional toll and the need for support systems for student reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance objective reporting with opinion commentary responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a clear distinction between news coverage and opinion pieces; use opinion sections to contextualize but not to substitute for rigorous reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper published opinion columns addressing solutions and critiques, noting that while opinion has a place, Erdely’s narrative style blurred lines and contributed to misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of hindsight and practice self-compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that retrospective judgments are easier than in-the-moment decisions; allow for learning and growth rather than harsh self-reproach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alumni reflected that 'hindsight is 20/20' and urged giving themselves 'a little bit of grace' about priorities, assumptions, and the pressures they faced as 18–21-year-old reporters.
